body.text: Recent reports of Chinese transgressions and resulting face-offs in Arunachal Pradesh, confirmed by the Director General of the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) on October 22, are yet another reminder that six years after Galwan, the border is quiet but neither at peace nor normal.

Since the October 2024 understanding on disengagement at Depsang and Demchok, there has been no restoration of the status quo that preceded the Chinese transgressions of May 2020 in eastern Ladakh, nor de-escalation or de-induction of troops. The 25th round of Special Representatives talks in August 2026 agreed to explore a debatable objective of an “Early and Substantial Harvest” in boundary delimitation, with a boundary settlement nowhere in sight. A militarised border with China, which refuses to clarify the Line of Actual Control (LAC), is the new normal, and India must plan for it as a long-term condition.

This essay makes three arguments. First, the Chinese challenge has changed in character in a strategic context that has shifted to its advantage: it is multi-domain, collusive, and backed by a widening gap in capability. Second, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) has real weaknesses, which India should study as closely as China studies those of other countries. Third, India’s answer lies not in parity, which it cannot achieve in the foreseeable future, but in asymmetric deterrence, backed by reforms that only political leadership can deliver.
THE CHALLENGE

First, the changed context. The US and China have recalibrated their relationship, seeking stability through frequent summits even as intense competition continues underneath. In practice, the US now treats China as a peer able to inflict pain it is not prepared to bear, and the balance has tilted towards China. This is not a G2, but it is a G2 overlay, in which the two may shape rules that affect India without its voice. The Democratic sweep of the US Congress on November 3 does not change this. The forces behind Donald Trump, from nativism to fatigue with foreign wars and support for tariffs, will outlast him. The 50 per cent tariffs of 2025 showed that the US will coerce a partner when it chooses. The India-US relationship is unlikely to recover its strategic mojo anytime soon. China, locked in a protracted contest with America, has reason to reduce friction with India while discouraging it from moving closer to the US, without accommodating its concerns. The recent thaw in India-China relations is tactical and reversible.
Risk of full-scale conflict is low

Second, it is probing, not war. The risk of a full-scale conflict with China in the near term is relatively low. The more likely scenario is Chinese probing along the LAC. In a Track 1.5 conversation, a Chinese scholar with a PLA background suggested that China has not yet reached its claim line in the western sector. In the eastern sector, China seeks an LAC based on literally transposing the small-scale maps of 1914, ignoring the watershed principle underlying the McMahon Line. Chinese attempts to alter the status quo to its advantage will continue and may intensify, as recent reports from Arunachal Pradesh suggest.

Third, the widening gap on the ground. China’s frenetic road and rail building is steadily cutting the time it needs to move forces to the border. The Lhasa-Nyingchi railway, opened in 2021, brought rail close to Arunachal Pradesh. A second highway through Aksai Chin, the G695, is planned to run parallel to the LAC by 2035. Permanent accommodation, hardened shelters, and fuel and ammunition depots now allow large forces to stay near the border through the winter. China has transformed Tibet from a remote frontier into an integrated military logistics platform.
Tibetan plateau and Chinese mainland

By 2035, the Tibetan plateau is likely to be connected to the Chinese heartland through rail corridors from Qinghai, Sichuan, and Xinjiang. The Sichuan-Tibet railway, now under construction, will augment military transportation capabilities opposite Arunachal Pradesh. The Xinjiang-Tibet railway, linking Hotan to Shigatse with sections close to the LAC, will bind western Tibet more closely to Xinjiang. The result will not simply be larger deployments but a sharp reduction in mobilisation time and a greater ability to sustain pressure simultaneously in Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh. Add 628 Xiaokang border villages, about 450 of them facing India’s north-eastern region, and China can induct forces in days where India often needs weeks.

India’s own efforts, including the Sela and Atal tunnels, the Darbuk-Shyok-DBO road, the upgrading of Nyoma, expanded Border Roads Organisation (BRO) activity, and the Vibrant Villages Programme, are a significant improvement over the past decade. Yet they remain catch-up measures against a Chinese system increasingly integrated across rail, road, air, and logistics.

Air power, long India’s trump card, is eroding as an advantage, though not disappearing. China has expanded and upgraded military and dual-use airfields across Tibet, with hardened shelters, advanced air defence, growing aerial refuelling, and deployment of J20 stealth fighters at Hotan and Damxung. The Indian Air Force is down to about 29 fighter squadrons against a sanctioned 42. India’s lower-altitude bases still offer real advantages, but China is steadily offsetting geography through technology. By 2035, the balance is likely to be decided less by runway altitude than by sensors, missiles, logistics, and the quality of multi-domain integration.

At sea, the PLA Navy has more than 370 ships and submarines and a ship-building capacity many times that of the US. A military-civil fusion channels commercial technology into the PLA. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) estimates China’s military spending in 2025 at $336 billion, against India’s $92.1 billion. The real gap is wider.

Then, there is the collusion. During Operation Sindoor in May 2025, according to the Deputy Chief of Army Staff, Pakistan had “live updates” from China on Indian deployments. China supplied satellite support and BeiDou navigation, helped Pakistan integrate its defence platforms, and used the conflict as a “live lab”. About 80 per cent of Pakistan’s military hardware is Chinese. The old two-front construct is being augmented by something subtler: one reinforced front. India may increasingly face a Chinese-enabled Pakistan, even as China stays below the threshold of direct intervention.

In fact, much of China’s pressure falls below the threshold of war: incremental intrusions, border villages, renaming places in Arunachal Pradesh, and projects on trans-border rivers. Chinese commentators now argue openly that China’s goal is to reach the so-called “LAC of November 7, 1959”, a notional alignment India has never accepted. Cyber intrusions into Indian networks signal access and disruption without inviting a military response. China’s new Aerospace, Cyberspace and Information Support Forces, set up in April 2024, and its pursuit of “intelligentised” warfare, with AI built into command, are part of China’s upgraded military doctrine. China has also invested heavily in “discourse power”, claiming that India is provocative while China is reasonable.

Finally, the nuclear shadow. China is moving from minimum deterrence towards a larger, more varied force meant to shape escalation. SIPRI put its stockpile at about 620 warheads in January 2026; the Pentagon expects more than 1,000 by 2030. China is shifting towards “early warning counterstrike”, and its strategic community suggests that its “No First Use” posture can be jettisoned under several circumstances. India, with a modest and less sophisticated arsenal, faces two nuclear neighbours with a long record of collusion. Basic nuclear stability between India and China is under growing stress.
THE PLA’S WEAKNESSES
The PLA also has weaknesses that India must understand and, where possible, exploit.

The purge of the PLA is without precedent since 1949 and has hollowed out the command. Over a hundred generals or equivalent have been removed since 2023. The Fifth Plenum of the 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China in October 2026 confirmed the expulsion of a record 33 members, 16 of them generals, including Zhang Youxia, the senior Vice Chairman of the Central Military Commission (CMC), and Liu Zhenli, Chief of Joint Staff. The CMC, meant to have 7 members, now has 2. All 5 theatre commands, including the Western Theatre facing India, have seen their leaders replaced.

Professional judgment is displaced by loyalty to President Xi Jinping. Promotions favour political reliability, and the newly promoted are themselves exposed to the next wave of purge. Authority, including over nuclear forces, is concentrated in one man. Officers who fear being the next target are less likely to take initiative or report bad news, a classic broken feedback loop. A command this thin and this recently reshuffled has never been tested in war.

A decade after the 2016 reforms, PLA jointness remains a work in progress. Most theatre commanders have been army officers, and the purge has disrupted the posts that matter most for joint operations.
China’s primary focus is the US, Taiwan, and the western Pacific. India is an adjunct threat in its planning. Any major commitment on the Himalayan front would weaken its hand in the east.
Equally,the PLA Navy’s ability to sustain a wartime force in the Indian Ocean is unproven, with distance, chokepoints, and limited bases being constraints.

The overall effect is mixed. Unit-level training, major exercises, infrastructure, ship-building, and nuclear expansion continue without pause. History also counsels caution: China entered Korea in 1950, attacked India in 1962, and fought the Soviet Union in 1969, during periods of intense internal turmoil. A politically insecure PLA, led by younger officers keen to prove their loyalty, may push harder at the border. The purge is a political earthquake that has made the terrain more unstable; it also raises questions about continuity of command and decision-making in a crisis.
THE RESPONSE

India cannot match China’s overall military power, and should not try. The aim should be to deny Chinese planners the confidence that coercion or limited war will bring quick and politically manageable gains. That calls for deterrence by denial, combined with deterrence by punishment. Every new railway and highway China builds into Tibet increases the temptation for India to respond symmetrically. That would be precisely the wrong lesson.

Ukraine and Iran show the efficacy of well-planned asymmetric response. Ukraine has held off a far larger adversary since 2022, using cheap drones in mass and long-range strikes deep inside Russia. Iran, attacked by the US and Israel from February 2026, did not need to close the Strait of Hormuz completely; it made passage uncertain and costly enough that ships stayed away. It changed deterrence dynamics by targeting Gulf countries. The lesson is that a state which understands its own advantages and its adversary’s vulnerabilities can impose costs out of proportion to its size.
Strategic risk: Neglecting the maritime dimension

The big strategic risk for India is to be bogged down on the land border and neglect the maritime dimension, where geography gives India its clearest advantage. Since 2020, the LAC has dominated Budget priorities, while the Navy and Air Force struggle for resources. Yet China, for the first time in centuries, faces no serious continental threat and is pouring resources into its navy. India must hold the line on land without weakening focus on the sea. That means a deliberate rebalancing of capital spending on maritime and air capabilities within an augmented defence budget.

The Andaman and Nicobar Islands sit astride the approaches to the Malacca Strait, through which most of China’s energy imports pass. This “Malacca card” warrants careful scrutiny. A blockade of Chinese shipping would be an act of major war and invite retaliation. China has spent two decades diversifying routes. Fixed bases on the islands are within reach of Chinese missiles. The utility of the Andaman option lies not in blockade but in uncertainty: persistent surveillance, tracking of Chinese submarines, and the ability, as Iran showed at Hormuz, to make passage risky and costly without formally closing anything. Investment should go into maritime domain awareness, anti-submarine networks, unmanned systems, and dispersed strike capability.

On land, the priority is denial: closing the infrastructure gap, hardening forward airfields and logistics, and building persistent surveillance along the LAC. The surprise of May 2020 was, at heart, a surveillance and assessment failure. For punishment, long-range systems such as BrahMos and Pralay can hold at risk the roads, railways, tunnels, depots, and airfields on which the PLA increasingly depends in Tibet. India’s objective should not be to match China’s infrastructure network but to retain the ability to disrupt it in crisis or conflict through precision conventional strikes, while augmenting its own infrastructure. Given China’s mix of nuclear and conventional missiles, a separate conventional rocket force would help keep India’s own lines clear. In the air, India needs a high-low mix: enough advanced fighters to restore squadron strength, alongside missiles, loitering munitions, and home-produced drones in large numbers, protected by layered air defence.

Grey zone coercion, aggressive action that falls between conventional peace and open war, is best met by area denial, quick attribution, and cost imposition. India needs early detection and pre-planned, proportionate responses. Above all, it needs candour. Keeping transgressions under wraps does not resolve them but encourages more. India also needs its own narrative and should call out China-Pakistan collusion plainly, rather than send mixed signals.

Moreover, critical networks, including power, finance, and nuclear grids, need further hardening. India should keep Chinese AI models out of government systems and critical infrastructure and avoid excessive dependence on the American stack, too. Algorithmic sovereignty, built on Indian compute, data, and models, must be part of national security.

While maintaining its no-first-use and credible minimum deterrence posture, the emphasis must be put on “credible”. What counts as minimum may need quiet upward revision. Continuous patrols by nuclear-armed submarines, longer-range sea-based missiles, and better early warning are priorities. India and China also need a channel to discuss nuclear risk, even at Track 2 level.

Defence alone will not deter a larger power that can choose the time and place of coercion. India needs options to embarrass China elsewhere if there is a repeat of the Galwan incident of eastern Ladakh: at different locations along the land border, through deeper partnerships with Vietnam, the Philippines, and Japan, and through a less inhibited approach to issues China considers sensitive.

None of this is possible without political direction. India has never published a National Security Strategy, despite several drafts. China, by contrast, sets out its strategic priorities regularly in defence White Papers. India’s defence spending fell from 17.1 per cent of Central government expenditure in 2014-15 to 13 per cent in 2025-26. The 2026-27 allocation of Rs.7.85 lakh crore lifts it only to 14.7 per cent, roughly 2 per cent of GDP. This is inadequate for a collusive two-front threat. The technology gap is equally concerning: India spends about 0.7 per cent of its GDP on research and development, against about 2.6 per cent in China.

India needs its own model of military-civil fusion, drawing in the private sector and start-ups through assured orders and faster trials. It needs dual and differentiated derisking of its economy: dual, because its vulnerabilities run to both China and the US, which have weaponised dependencies; differentiated, because not all dependencies carry equal risk. The Agnipath scheme was a self-goal; the Cabinet’s decision of November 4, 2026, to extend service by two years is a partial and piecemeal correction. India cannot allow its border areas to empty out while China increases settlements; the Vibrant Villages Programme must be stepped up.

Crucially, a multi-domain war cannot be fought by three services that plan separately. History shows that militaries rarely restructure themselves. In the US, it took the Goldwater-Nichols Act of 1986, pushed through by Congress against opposition from the Pentagon and service chiefs, to create genuinely joint commands. In China, Xi personally drove the reforms of 2015-16, ending the PLA Army’s dominance and replacing seven military regions with five theatre commands. India created the post of Chief of Defence Staff in 2019. Seven years later, theatre commands remain elusive; in October 2026, the Defence Secretary said a blueprint was “awaiting approval at the highest level”. Only the political leadership can settle questions such as the wartime chain of command and air assets. India should build its own model, but the decision cannot wait.

Finally, while partnerships with the US, Europe, Japan, and Australia matter, no partner will fight India’s continental battles, and the US will strike its own bargains with China. The litmus test for any partnership is whether it helps India build its own capabilities.

India has faced steeper odds before. It rebuilt its defences after 1962, responded with resolve at Nathu La in 1967, and stood firm at Sumdorong Chu (1986), Doklam (2017), and eastern Ladakh (2020). Deterrence is not the dividend of parity. It is the product of strategic clarity, accurate assessment of the situation, careful planning, and the determination to act with discipline and despatch. The challenge India faces today is no longer the China of 1962 or even of 2020, but a China that is steadily integrating military, technological, and logistical power across domains. Deterring a stronger neighbour requires India to think and act with the same long-term strategic focus and determination.
Ashok K. Kantha, a former Ambassador of India to China, is the Subhas Chandra Bose Chair Professor of International Relations, Chanakya University, Bengaluru.
